_how: The crew as data. One entry per division, one per worker. Adding a worker is adding an entry here: 'impl' names its implementation in workers.IMPLS, 'provider' names an entry in 'providers' (the minimum seconds between two requests to that host, shared by every worker on it). Worker ids are '<division>.<name>' and must be unique; an unknown field, impl, provider or division is an error at load time. Moss is not in this file: she is a separate process (C:\src\Galatea) that reads the leaders' reports and sets each division's goal and compute share.

divisions.title: Posting
divisions.leader_notes: Three workers post: posting.blog (blog posts on the website), posting.instagram (Instagram card posts) and posting.devto (each published blog post cross-posted to dev.to, unchanged). Each row names its worker; report them separately. Each worker's post.tally holds its counts: drafts written, drafts blocked, posts submitted for approval, posts pending approval, posts published, posts denied (for posting.devto: cross-posts, and published blog posts waiting to be cross-posted). A post PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been published: say it is waiting for the owner's approval, never that it is out. Only a post.published row is a published post; give its URL for the blog and dev.to, its permalink for Instagram. A post.blocked row is a draft the content check stopped before anyone saw it: say so and give its reasons by kind (a name not on the allowlist, a link or domain, personal data, a business number, an internal system name, text that does not fit the Instagram card) without repeating any name the reasons quote. A post.not_published row says why a submitted post did not go out (denied by the owner, failed, or done without a URL or permalink). posting.results reads the site's own visit counter for the last 30 days: traffic.working is the plain summary (read it first), traffic.site the site and each channel (blog links, instagram bio, dev.to, search), traffic.posts each published post by its slug (page views, clicks to product pages, dev.to visits, sales), traffic.sales sales and net revenue per campaign. Use these figures to suggest which topics to do more of, naming each post by its slug with its figures as recorded. Say what the numbers show, never why: one post doing well is not proof that its topic caused it, so never claim cause from one data point. A post with fewer than 20 page views is too early to tell: say so, and draw nothing from it. A figure marked 'at least' is a lower bound, and a post listed as unknown has no number: never write it as zero. When traffic.working says there is no traffic data yet, say exactly that and suggest nothing about topics.

divisions.title: Contracts
divisions.leader_notes: Three workers: contracts.orders, the order desk, contracts.delivery, the delivery desk, and contracts.finder, the finder; each row names its worker, report them separately. The order desk reads the client orders for paid 'I do it for you' work and answers each by a fixed template (an acknowledgement, a quote acknowledgement or a decline), each parked for the owner's approval before it is sent. Report NEW PAID ORDERS first and prominently: they are money. Each order.new_paid row is one, with its order id, package and amount as recorded. order.tally holds the counts: orders by status, paid orders waiting for acknowledgement, paid orders held for the owner, acknowledgements sent, quote acknowledgements sent, quote requests waiting for the owner, flagged orders awaiting the owner, declines sent, refunds to issue by hand in Stripe, abandoned checkouts, paid revenue in the orders listed, and client emails pending the owner's approval, denied, failed and blocked. An email PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent: say it is waiting for the owner. Only an order.email_sent row is a sent email. Never promise a client anything, and never state a price, a date, a turnaround or a delivery beyond what the rows record: the desk sends only its fixed templates. Flagged orders (the brief matched a category the owner declines, named in the row's flags) and quote requests need the owner: say so with their order ids, and say that a flag is only a flag until the owner approves the decline. Paid orders held for the owner (a package or amount the templates do not cover) need him too. Refunds are never automated: a declined paid order is a refund the owner issues by hand in Stripe, so say how many are waiting. When the orders could not be read, say they are UNKNOWN, never zero. contracts.delivery ships each order's finished work: the owner drops a zip in the order's folder, and the desk submits it as a delivery email with a private download link, parked for the owner's approval. delivery.tally holds the counts: orders in progress, orders in progress with no delivery yet (waiting for a zip), orders past their turnaround, deliveries pending the owner's approval, deliveries delivered, revised deliveries delivered, deliveries blocked by the checks, deliveries denied, failed, and approved deliveries that failed to send (offered to the owner again). A delivery PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been delivered, and nothing is delivered until a delivery.delivered row says so: never say or imply a client has their work before that row. A delivery.blocked row is URGENT for the owner: Pionir's checks refused the zip before anyone saw it (for example a secret found in it, an executable, or no README or HOWTO); give the order id and the reason, and say the client is still waiting until he drops a fixed zip - the same zip is never tried again. The tally's blocked list holds each blocked order's reason. Orders past their turnaround are late: say so with their order ids. When the orders could not be read, the deliveries are UNKNOWN, never 'nothing to deliver'. contracts.finder handles 'Find it for me' orders ($19 flat, a report of where to buy something within 2 business days, a full refund if nothing is found): once the order desk's acknowledgement is sent, it asks Claude to research the item on the web (counted against the daily Claude cap), checks the answer, and submits the client's report, parked for the owner's approval. find.tally holds the counts: find orders in progress, find orders waiting for research, find orders waiting for Claude budget, research runs, research failures, find reports pending the owner's approval, find reports sent, not-found reports sent, refunds to issue by hand in Stripe, find reports blocked, denied and failed. A find.research_failed row is URGENT for the owner: Claude's research was missing or failed the checks twice (or the brief must not be researched), nothing was sent, and the client is waiting - give the order id and the reasons. A find.report_blocked row is URGENT too: the report was refused before anyone saw it; give the order id and the reason, and say it is never resent. Orders waiting for Claude budget are waiting, not skipped: say so. A report PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent; only a find.report_sent row is a sent report. A not-found report sent is a refund the owner issues by hand in Stripe: say how many are waiting. Never promise a client a price, a stock level or a find: prices and stock are the sellers', they change, and only the report states them.

divisions.title: Products
divisions.leader_notes: products.shelf puts the products the owner stages on sale on Gumroad, each only after the owner approves it on Discord, and reads what the live ones sold. Report NEW SALES first and prominently: they are money. Each product.new_sales row is one product whose sales count rose since the last look, with its slug, the new sales and its totals as Gumroad reports them. A product.blocked row is URGENT for the owner: Pionir's checks refused the product before anyone saw it (for example a secret found in the zip, no README, an executable, a cover too small); give its slug, version and the reason, and say it stays off sale until he stages fixed files - the same content is never tried again. The tally's blocked list holds each blocked product's reason. A product.listing_malformed row, and the tally's malformed list, is a listing.json that failed the shelf's own check and was NOT submitted: give the folder and the reasons. Never call a product live, on sale or published until a product.published row says so (or product.sales lists it as live): a product PENDING APPROVAL is waiting for the owner and is NOT on sale. A product.not_published row says why a submitted product did not go out (denied by the owner, failed, or an approved one that failed to publish and will be offered to him again). product.tally holds the counts: products staged, staged but not yet approved, pending the owner's approval, blocked by the checks, denied by the owner, malformed listings, failed, and product versions published. product.sales holds each live product's sales and revenue as Gumroad reports them (stream = the product's slug), and the totals (stream all). When the newest row is product.sales_unavailable, the sales and revenue are UNKNOWN, never zero: say so. Suggest a price or listing change only from the sales recorded in product.sales, naming the product by its slug with its figures as recorded; never invent a sale, a price or a trend, and never claim why a product sold. With no sales recorded yet, say exactly that and suggest nothing about prices.

workers.name: shelf
workers.note: each product staged in its own folder published on Gumroad, for the owner's approval, and the live products' sales as Gumroad reports them; no model
